label: bm-wood-cellulose-hygromorphs
topic: Wood and cellulose hygromorphs in architecture: measured benchmarks (curvature, layer ratios, strain, speed, cycles, Timoshenko error) that a new biomaterial must beat
summary: Fetched and read in full this run: Holstov et al. 2015 (Newcastle open copy), Correa et al. 2015 (MIT open copy, the MIT Self-Assembly Lab / Stuttgart ICD paper), Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015, Gronquist 2018 and 2019, Cheng et al. 2024, Kruger 2021, Dingler 2021, Khoshtinat 2023 (cellulose acetate), Tseo 2025 (bacterial-cellulose preprint), Peng 2023, plus the ICD project pages for HygroSkin and HygroScope. Benchmarks. Wood bilayers reach 4.5-8.7 m^-1 in about 24-48 h at 4.7-8 mm total thickness (Ruggeberg 2015; Gronquist 2018). Printed cellulose/polyketone bilayers reach 15.5 m^-1 at 80% RH, switch fully in 30 min, survive 170 cycles and 13 months on a facade mock-up (Cheng 2024). A 0.23 mm cellulose-acetate/tape bilayer reaches 51.1 m^-1 (Khoshtinat 2023). Veneer elements in HygroSkin close 'within a few minutes' (ICD page; no thickness or curvature published there). Size sets speed: a 1 mm birch veneer on 0.2 mm glass-fibre reaches 80% of its curvature in 2 h 15 min in humid air (Holstov 2015); 4.1 mm beech needs 12.6-18.8 h for 80% moisture change (my recomputation of the ETH data); 15-45 mm mass timber needs 400-900+ h (Gronquist 2019). No measured wood bilayer I could quantify exceeds kappa*h/d_eps = 1.5; the six ETH beech bilayers give 0.91-1.53. Timoshenko accuracy. Within 5-13% for stiff wood bilayers at near-optimal layer ratio, but at 1:1 thickness the model overpredicts by my calculation; +26% for soft cellulose acetate (analytic 0.0645 vs measured 0.0511 mm^-1); about 4x for 6 um polymer films (Dingler 2021); 2.5-9x off in fitted modulus ratio for printed wood-filament (Kruger 2021); and a fitted correction factor C = 1.72 for bacterial-cellulose bilayers (Tseo 2025). Contradiction of the earlier record: the 3/2 ceiling is NOT a new result. Holstov et al. 2015 plotted f(m,n) over many modulus ratios and wrote that its maximum 'remains constant at 1.5'; what is new in this project is the kernel-checked proof and the exact optimum m = n^-1/2. Also: bacterial-cellulose bilayers in the literature I found are driven by heat-drying (90-120 C), not ambient humidity, and the one preprint also moulds its cellulose in Formlabs Rigid 10K printed parts. Hard gaps: HygroSkin/HygroScope layer thicknesses, curvatures and cycle counts are in paywalled papers I could not read.
lay_summary: Thin strips of wood or paper curl when the air gets damp or dry, because one side swells more than the other. Think of a wet pine cone closing and a dry one opening. Architects at Stuttgart used this to build walls whose holes open and shut with the weather, with no motors. We collected the best measurements to date, so any new material can be compared fairly. A strip of wood a few millimetres thick takes about a day to bend, while a sheet thinner than a sheet of card can bend in under an hour. Printed wood-fibre plastic survived 170 damp-dry rounds and 13 months outside. The simple bending formula from 1925 works within about 10 percent for stiff wood but can be off by a factor of four for soft, thin films. One surprise: the best possible bend for a given swelling was already known as a plotted limit in 2015, so our contribution is the computer-checked proof, not the limit itself.

glossary.plain: A material that changes shape when the air humidity changes.
Two thin layers glued face to face, one that swells and one that does not, so the strip curls.
How tightly a strip bends; 10 per metre means a circle of radius 10 cm.
How much more one layer would swell than the other if they were not glued together.
The 1925 equation that predicts how much a two-layer strip bends from its layer thicknesses, stiffnesses and swelling.
The most a strip can bend is 1.5 times the swelling difference divided by the strip thickness, whatever the stiffnesses.

glossary.term: thickness ratio m, modulus ratio n
glossary.plain: Passive-layer thickness divided by active-layer thickness, and passive stiffness divided by active stiffness.
Time to reach 80 percent of the final bend.
How damp the air is, as a percentage of the most water vapour it can hold.
A very thin sliver of wood, usually under 2 mm.
Fused filament fabrication, the common hobby 3D printer that melts plastic thread.
A wet, felt-like cellulose sheet grown by bacteria in a tray.
A single number for how fast water soaks through a material, worked out from how long a sample took to respond.
The small trusted program that checks a mathematical proof step by step.

findings.claim: The 3/2 ceiling on Timoshenko's coefficient was already stated numerically in the architecture-hygromorph literature in 2015: Holstov et al. plotted f(m,n) for many stiffness ratios and report that its maximum is the same, 1.5, for every ratio, reached at a different thickness ratio each time. Their Figure 11 marks the f=1.5 line as the optimal (m,n) combinations. They did not prove it.
findings.value: max f = 1.5 for all n (plotted, not proved)
findings.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5 and in each case is achieved at single yet different thickness ratio

findings.claim: CONTRADICTS spec-hygromorph-4d.json, which called the bound 'my own derivation rather than a literature finding'. The numerical ceiling is in Holstov 2015, and Dingler 2021 also states 'global maxima'. What remains new is the proof (Lean kernel) and the closed-form optimum m = n^-1/2. The grid check in benchmarks.py (n from 1e-3 to 1e3, m from 1e-3 to 1e3) gives max f = 1.5000000000000002 with the optimum within 2% of n^-1/2 each time; this is a numerical check only.
findings.value: grid max f = 1.5; optimum m = n^-1/2

findings.claim: Holstov's worked example (wood 0.5 GPa across grain, fibreglass 15 GPa) puts the optimum at a passive layer about 5 times thinner than the active one. Recomputed: n = 30, m = 0.2 gives f = 1.498 (99.9% of the ceiling); the n^-1/2 optimum is m = 0.183. At equal thickness f = 0.545, a 64% loss against the paper's 'as much as 60%'.
findings.evidence_quote: If the layers were of equal thickness, for the same overall thickness of the composite the response would be reduced by as much as 60%.

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 measured speed on 150 x 100 mm samples, 1 mm rotary-cut birch active layer with 0.2 mm fibreglass passive layer: 80% of the curvature change in about 30 min when sprayed with liquid water, but about 2 h 15 min when the change is a humid-air step (wetting and drying alike). Curvature values were in figures only and could not be read.
findings.value: t80 = 0.5 h (liquid), 2.25 h (humid air), active layer 1 mm
findings.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 says quarter-cut veneer, the type used by the Stuttgart HygroScope/HygroSkin work, responds less than plain-cut or rotary-cut veneer, because rotary-cut aligns the tangential (largest) swelling with the plane.
findings.evidence_quote: Hygromorphs with active layers of plain-cut and rotary-cut wood veneer are more responsive than those with quarter-cut veneer active layers.

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 gives two durability constraints that matter for architecture: wood preservatives and fire retardants destroy hygroscopicity, and thin wood layers erode at 2-10 mm per century outdoors (so a 1 mm layer has a short life).
findings.evidence_quote: many wood processing methods, including the application of fire-retardants and coatings and impregnated preservatives aimed to protect wood against weathering, usually result in irreversible loss of its hygroscopicity

findings.claim: Holstov 2015 saw a first-cycle effect: thin wood layers prepared dry shrink below their start size after the first wet-dry cycle, so the dry shape of cycle 1 differs from later cycles. The authors suspect irreversible compressive strain in the veneer.
findings.evidence_quote: composites with thin active wood layers prepared in dry conditions exhibit a difference between the first and the subsequent response cycles

findings.claim: HygroSkin (ICD, 2013): quarter-cut maple veneer composite apertures respond over 30-90% RH; 28 unique components with 1100 apertures; open-to-closed 'within a few minutes' for a rapid RH rise; reversibility verified in 'a large number of long-term tests' with no count, thickness or curvature on the page. The <0.5 mm figure is geometric accuracy of the self-formed plywood shell, not actuator performance.
findings.evidence_quote: In this project the elements change from open to closed within a few minutes given a rapid rise in relative humidity.

findings.claim: HygroScope (ICD, Centre Pompidou 2012): more than 4000 unique elements of quarter-cut maple veneer plus synthetic composites, programmed by five parameters including the humidity at which the element is produced. The page gives no curvature, thickness or time.
findings.evidence_quote: More than 4000 geometrically unique elements are digitally fabricated and the complex substructure is robotically manufactured.

findings.claim: MIT Self-Assembly Lab / ICD printed wood (Correa 2015): a wood-filament sample 20 x 100 mm needs 12 h to transform fully in submersion, with the reverse 15 min to 2 h depending on RH; the wood/ABS net needs 12-24 h in high humidity to saturate and repeated over 30 cycles without visible degradation; the authors state both methods take very long in water vapour compared with submersion.
findings.evidence_quote: A sample of 20 mm by 100 mm will reach full transformation under full submersion after 12 h; the reverse cycle is faster and can range from 15 min to 2 h, depending on the R.H.

findings.claim: Correa 2015 wood/nylon multimaterial prints fold 104-110 degrees in 1.5-12 min but only by water or heat, and the folding angle shrinks with each cycle, so they are not a durable humidity actuator.
findings.value: 104-110 deg in 1.5-2 min (air-dry) or 10-12 min (heat); angle falls per cycle
findings.evidence_quote: However, the folding angle gradually decreases with each transformation cycle

findings.claim: Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 (beech 4 mm active, spruce 0.2-4 mm passive, 120 mm long, RH 85->35%): curvature up to 8.7e-3 mm^-1 (8.7 m^-1) for spruce up to 1 mm and 1.5e-3 mm^-1 (1.5 m^-1) for 4 mm spruce after 24 h; computed tip angle 59 deg vs measured 55 deg. Confirms the earlier agent's numbers.
findings.value: 8.7 m^-1 and 1.5 m^-1 at 24 h; 59 vs 55 deg
findings.evidence_quote: For bilayers with a thickness of the spruce layer up to 1mm, curvatures up to 8.7*10-3mm-1 were reached, whereas bilayers with a spruce layer of 4mm thickness reached a curvature of 1.5*10-3 mm-1 after 24 hours only.

findings.claim: Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 Timoshenko error under cycling: +11% and +13% for the 0.2 mm and 0.8 mm spruce bilayers, under 5% for the other two. Confirms the earlier agent.
findings.evidence_quote: For the bilayers with 0.2mm and 0.8mm thick spruce layers, the specific curvatures slightly increased over time and were 11% and 13% higher than the calculated values.

findings.claim: DEEPENS the earlier record: using the paper's own coefficients (beech 3.2e-3, spruce 0.07e-3 per %MC), a moisture drop of 8 points (18 to 10) and n = 10, 20, 30, Timoshenko gives 6.3-7.9 m^-1 for 0.2-1.0 mm spruce (the measured 'up to 8.7' is 10-28% higher) but 1.7-3.1 m^-1 for 4 mm spruce (m = 1) against 1.5 measured, i.e. +14% (n=30) to +108% (n=10). The paper says the 24 h values 'match' in its Fig. 2e, which I could not read, so this is a check of the 'matches' claim, not a refutation. The earlier agent checked only m = 0.2.

Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 outdoor test: untreated bilayers carrying 100 g and 150 g tip loads ran nine months from July 2013; specific curvature stayed 3-4e-4 mm^-1 per %RH to January 2014, fell to 2-3e-4 in February-April 2014, despite visible splitting and cracking from UV and rain.
findings.evidence_quote: although splitting and cracking of the wood due to the impact of UV-radiation and rain became visible, the amplitude of actuation has only slightly decreased over time.

findings.claim: Gronquist 2018 thin beech bilayers (120 x 20 mm, 35% RH, 48 h): maximum 4.5 m^-1 at r = 0.17 and minimum 1.5 m^-1 at r = 0.49; model error below 10% at r = 0.34, slightly under-predicting at low r and over-predicting at high r.
findings.evidence_quote: A maximum of κd ≈ 4.5 m−1 was reached for r = 0.17 and a minimum of κd ≈ 1.5 m−1 was reached for r = 0.49 after 48 hours in 35% r.h. climate

findings.claim: Recomputed from the ETH data (six beech bilayers, three samples each): kappa*h/d_eps = 1.35, 1.50, 1.53, 1.36, 1.04, 0.91 for r = 0.13-0.49, confirming the earlier scout figures (1.35-1.53 and 0.91). Moisture half-time 2.8-4.8 h, 80% time 12.6-18.8 h for the 4.1 mm active layer; curvature t80 11.9-19.1 h. Caveat: d_eps uses nominal swelling coefficients (0.0019 and 0.0001 per %MC), so 1.53 is within their stated uncertainty of the ceiling.

Gronquist 2019 mass timber: bilayers 15, 30 and 45 mm; moisture about equilibrated at 400 h, but not at 900 h for 45 mm; the model fairly predicts beech but overestimates spruce curvature; adhesive thickness, stiffness and shear modulus do not influence shape.
findings.evidence_quote: WMCs were approximately equilibrated after 400 hours in the dry target climate, except for the bilayer series with a thickness of 45 mm, for which an equilibration is not visible after 900 hours.

findings.claim: Urbach Tower (14 m, ICD/ITKE): panels were made flat at 22% wood moisture and dried to 12% to curve; only the press report gives this, no radius or lamella thickness was found.
findings.evidence_quote: The panels were manufactured flat and with a high wood-moisture content of 22 per cent.

findings.claim: Vailati et al. 2017 (abstract only; full text paywalled): wood bilayers up to half a metre wide curved only along their length, and milling grooves into the active layer sped moisture change and curvature change, especially under cyclic RH.
findings.value: width up to 0.5 m; grooves raise rate
findings.evidence_quote: The milling of grooves increased the moisture change rate substantially compared to the non-milled samples resulting in a higher rate of curvature change.

findings.claim: Peng et al. 2023 (veneer-scale wood bilayers): a 200 um passive layer on a 400 um active layer at 0.6% initial moisture was the most sensitive to RH; hysteresis between adsorption and desorption grows at lower thickness ratio; behaviour repeatable after the first cycle. Numerical curvatures were in figures I did not read.
findings.evidence_quote: the bilayer composed of a 200 μm passive layer and a 400 μm active layer with 0.6% iMC was found to be the most sensitive to RH change

findings.claim: Cheng et al. 2024 (printed cellulose/polyketone bilayers): mean curvature 0.0155 mm^-1 (15.5 m^-1; radius 64.5 mm, own arithmetic 1/0.0155) at 80% RH independent of temperature; 170 cycles between 30% and 90% RH with slight loss only in the first ten; full 30<->90% RH change within 30 min; 13-month facade mock-up; 424 modules, 1.4% replaced after cycle testing. Confirms the earlier agent. Layer thicknesses are only in the supplement, which I did not read, so kappa*h/d_eps cannot be computed.
findings.evidence_quote: At the high RH of 90%, there is some slight reduction in bilayer curvature within the first ten cycles of actuation; in the following 160 cycles, the bilayer curvatures remain generally consistent

findings.claim: CORRECTS a detail in spec-hygromorph-4d.json: for Kruger 2021 (Laywood/PLA) the original Timoshenko model fits only with modulus ratio n = 111.6-286.0, the width-corrected model with n = 299.7-691.2 (Table 2); the earlier '150-690' blends the two. Measured n is 25-60 (dry/humid), not '~40'. The authors say measured curvatures could not be reproduced computationally because non-linear material behaviour is missing.
findings.evidence_quote: Although the observed experimental values could not be reproduced computationally, because the potentially non-linear material behavior is not accounted for in the model

findings.claim: Cellulose acetate on tape (Khoshtinat 2023, open access): h_a 86 um, h_p 145 um, total 0.228 mm, RH 35->80%. Measured curvature 0.0511 mm^-1 (R 19.56 mm), finite element 0.0519 mm^-1, analytic Timoshenko 0.0645 mm^-1 (R 15.5 mm), i.e. +26% over experiment; authors blame moisture-softening of the film. FE saturation time for 86 um from dry, one face open: about 60 min.
findings.evidence_quote: The analytical model, on the other hand, estimates a final curvature of only 0.0645 mm −1 (R = 15.5 mm), resulting in a 3.43 mm difference in bending radius from the experiment.

findings.claim: Own calculation on the cellulose-acetate bilayer using the authors' m = 1.69 and n = 3.84: f = 0.981, only 65% of the 1.5 ceiling; the n^-1/2 optimum would be m = 0.51, so the passive layer is about 3.3 times too thick. Even so the film makes 51.1 m^-1 because it is 0.228 mm thick; the ceiling implies a free differential strain of at least 0.78%.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py using m, n and kappa from https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10570-023-05342-1

findings.claim: Bacterial cellulose, Tseo et al. 2025 preprint (not peer reviewed): BC bimorph strips follow the Timoshenko equation 'adapted for hydrogels' only with a correction factor (C = 1.72, optimised separately for each bimorph); trajectory error 1.9 +/- 0.6 mm. Actuation is dehydration at 120 C (strips) or 90 C (multi-layer figure, 80 min), not ambient humidity.
findings.evidence_quote: comparing observed trajectories with model predictions across all constructed bimorphs yields a consistently low mean-squared error of 1.9 mm ± 0.6 mm

findings.claim: Same preprint: untreated BC pellicles took 1070 min to reach dry weight against 70-90 min for NaOH/BslA-treated ones; a 0.37 g BC gripper held 135 g; the gripper moulds were 3D-printed in Formlabs Rigid 10K and the pellicle grown inside them, a direct Formlabs-resin route for cellulose shaping. No cycle count or curvature in m^-1 is reported.
findings.value: 1070 vs 70-90 min; 0.37 g holds 135 g; Rigid 10K mould
findings.evidence_quote: we first 3D printed molds of the shape out of autoclavable UV cured resin (Formlabs, Rigid 10K)

findings.claim: Paper/CMC bilayers (Seelinger 2024) deviate about 15% from finite-element prediction at 10 wt% CMC, worse above 20 wt%, and miss the start position by 5-6 mm after cycling between 10% and 90% RH. Confirms the earlier agent; curvature numbers are in figures only.
findings.evidence_quote: Here, the deviation from the observed experimental results to the FEA results is approx. 15%.

findings.claim: Dingler 2021 confirmed: 17 um bilayer measured 1.2 mm^-1, 54 um bilayer about three times lower; Timoshenko with measured inputs gives 1.6 mm^-1 for the 54 um film. The paper's own sentence lists its 'global maxima' as 1.7 and 5.4 mm^-1 for '17 and 54 um', which is reversed: 1.5 x 0.061 / 0.017 mm = 5.4 mm^-1 belongs to the 17 um film. The earlier agent's numbers stand.
findings.evidence_quote: The global maxima generally achievable for 17 and 54 µm bilayers would be κ = 1.7 and 5.4 mm–1, respectively.

findings.claim: Apparent diffusivity from response times (slab with one face open, Fourier numbers 0.197, 0.567, 1.129 for 50%, 80%, 95% uptake): Holstov 1 mm birch t80 = 2.25 h gives 0.25 mm^2/h (7e-11 m^2/s) one-sided or 0.063 mm^2/h two-sided; ETH 4.1 mm beech moisture t50 gives 0.24 mm^2/h (two faces) to 0.95 mm^2/h (one face); cellulose acetate 86 um at 95% in 60 min gives 0.0084 mm^2/h. The earlier spec-bilayer-physics.json filament range was 0.001-0.015 mm^2/h, so wood veneer is roughly 4-1000 times faster per unit area than those printed resins. Treat as order of magnitude: moisture t80/t50 in the ETH data is 4.5, not the Fickian 2.9.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py (apparent_diffusivity) from Holstov 2015, the ETH csv and Khoshtinat 2023
findings.value: wood veneer D_app 0.06-0.95 mm^2/h; CA 0.008 mm^2/h

findings.claim: What the benchmarks demand of a new material, via the ceiling d_eps >= (2/3) kappa h: matching wood (8.7 m^-1) at h = 0.8 mm needs a free differential strain of at least 0.46%; matching printed cellulose (15.5 m^-1) needs 0.83% (1.65% at 1.6 mm); matching cellulose acetate (51.1 m^-1) needs 2.73% at 0.8 mm (1.36% at 0.4 mm). Project-record stock Flexible 80A V2 (0.99% immersion strain at 1 day) caps at 18.6 m^-1 at 0.8 mm, so it can just match printed cellulose but only after immersion, not humid air.
findings.source: own calculation benchmarks.py (strain_needed_for_benchmark_curvature); Flexible 80A figure from agents/scout-biomaterial.json (project record)

findings.claim: Across the bilayers with enough data, only designs near n^-1/2 approach the ceiling: Holstov worked example 99.9%, Dingler 98.9%, ETH beech at r=0.17-0.22 100-102%, cellulose acetate 65%, Dingler's measured curvature only 33-37% of the ceiling at its reported 6.1% strain, Ruggeberg m=1 about 47% by theory. A new material's score should be reported as kappa*h/d_eps, not raw curvature.

key_claims.claim: The maximum of Timoshenko's coefficient is 1.5 for every modulus ratio, and was already shown numerically by Holstov et al. 2015, so the project's novelty is the machine-checked proof, not the bound.
key_claims.evidence_quote: Plotting f(m,n) for a wide range of possible stiffness ratios shows that the maximum value of the function remains constant at 1.5 and in each case is achieved at single yet different thickness ratio

key_claims.claim: Measured curvature benchmarks: wood 4.5-8.7 m^-1 in 24-48 h at 4.7-8 mm; printed cellulose composite 15.5 m^-1, 30 min, 170 cycles, 13 months on a facade; cellulose acetate film 51.1 m^-1 at 0.228 mm.
key_claims.evidence_quote: The bilayers reach a full transformation between two RH extremes of 30% and 90% within 30 minutes

key_claims.claim: Timoshenko error depends on stiffness and softness: +5 to +13% for stiff wood near the optimum, +26% for cellulose acetate, about 4x for thin soft polymer films, fitted modulus ratio 2.5-9x too high for printed wood-filament, and a fitted correction factor 1.72 for bacterial cellulose.
key_claims.evidence_quote: For the other two bilayers differences between experimentally derived and calculated specific curvature were less than 5%.

key_claims.claim: Response time rises steeply with thickness: 30 min (printed, thin), 2 h 15 min (1 mm birch veneer in humid air), 12.6-18.8 h (4.1 mm beech, 80% moisture change), 400-900+ h (15-45 mm timber). Anything meant to beat wood at 1 mm and above must clear about 2 h for 80%.
key_claims.source: https://doi.org/10.25405/ncl.34238076 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6744262/ ; own calculation on ETH csv
key_claims.evidence_quote: 80% of the total curvature change in both the transfer from dry conditions to humid and vice-versa is achieved in approximately 2 hours 15 minutes

could_not_find: HygroSkin and HygroScope layer thicknesses, measured curvatures, modulus or swelling values, and any cycle count: the primary papers (Reichert et al. 2015 CAD; Menges & Reichert 2015 AD; Correa et al. 2013 ACADIA; Wood et al. 2018) are paywalled or blocked and only the ICD project pages (RH range 30-90%, 'a few minutes', 1100 apertures, >4000 elements) were readable. The 'few minutes' figure carries no thickness, so it cannot be compared with Holstov's 2 h 15 min.

Numeric curvature for Holstov 2015 (Figures 8, 12, 13) and for the Ruggeberg & Burgert 2015 Fig. 2e curve: figures only, values not read, so the Timoshenko comparison in my own calculation is from the paper's coefficients and not from its plot.

Any peer-reviewed bacterial-cellulose bilayer driven by ambient relative humidity with measured curvature, thickness ratio and cycle count. Five Europe PMC and Crossref queries and one extended web search found only: the Tseo 2025 preprint (heat-drying at 90-120 C), review articles, and a TCNF/reduced-graphene-oxide bilayer (Heraly 2022, Wiley, HTTP 403, so only a web-search snippet: 0.92 s recovery, 90% curvature retained after 100 cycles; NOT verified and not used as a finding).

Cycle count or fatigue life for bacterial cellulose, cellulose acetate, and for HygroSkin; the highest verified counts are 170 (Cheng 2024, printed cellulose composite), about 12 loops (Ruggeberg 2015), over 30 (Correa 2015) and a 13-month facade mock-up.
Cheng 2024 layer thicknesses (Supplementary Table 1) and the numeric files in its Figshare archive (over the 20 MB download limit): kappa*h/d_eps for the printed cellulose bilayer cannot be computed.

MIT Self-Assembly Lab measured curvature versus humidity for wood veneer (only Correa 2015 and, from the earlier record, Raviv 2014 which is immersion-driven material jetting); no SAL page with numbers was reachable and I did not re-fetch Raviv 2014.
Urbach Tower panel radius and lamella thickness: the Empa page returned HTTP 403; only Dezeen (22% to 12% moisture, 14 m) and the Stuttgart press PDF.
Peng 2023 and Seelinger 2024 curvature values (figures only); Vailati 2017/2018 and Wood 2018 numbers (paywalled; abstract only for Vailati 2017).
The original Timoshenko 1925 text; the formula was taken from the project record and from three papers that print it (Holstov, Khoshtinat, Tseo), which agree in form.

A hygromorph benchmark measured on a vat-printed (SLA) or powder-bed (SLS) part: none appears in any source read; the nearest Formlabs link is Tseo 2025 using Rigid 10K printed moulds only for growing cellulose, not as an actuator.
Tools not run: no Lean process was started; the 3/2 grid check is Python floating point and is not a proof.
recommendations: Stop describing the 3/2 ceiling as a new result in anything shown to Mamou-Mani or in a paper; cite Holstov et al. 2015 (numerical, plotted) and present the Lean-checked proof plus the optimum m = n^-1/2 as the contribution.

Report every new bilayer as kappa*h/d_eps with d_eps measured on free-swelling coupons of the same print, alongside raw curvature. Literature efficiency spans 0.33 (thin polymer film) to about 1.5 (tuned wood), so raw curvature hides design quality.

Set the bar to beat: curvature >= 15.5 m^-1 at the same RH step as Cheng 2024 (needs d_eps >= 0.83% at 0.8 mm), t80 under 2 h at 1 mm in humid air (Holstov), 170 humid cycles with <10% loss (Cheng), and a Timoshenko prediction within 10% using humidity-dependent moduli.

Choose the passive layer so that m = n^-1/2 (about 0.18 for a 30:1 stiffness ratio) and check that this thickness is printable (0.2 mm minimum wall on Form 4 per the earlier record); the cellulose-acetate bilayer lost 35% of its possible curvature by being 3.3x too thick on the passive side.

Expect Timoshenko to overpredict for soft, thin or highly swelling layers (+26% to 4x in the sources); plan to fit with humidity-dependent modulus and report the error, since the benchmark papers that do so are the ones that agree within 10%.

Keep the active layer thin: wood needs 12-19 h at 4 mm and 400+ h at 15 mm, so thickness, not chemistry, dominates speed; grooves or perforations (Vailati 2017) and one-sided passive layers (Holstov) are the proven speed-ups.

Bacterial cellulose grown in Form 4 Rigid 10K moulds (Tseo 2025) is a low-risk first demonstrator of cellulose shaping on Formlabs hardware, but it needs a humid-air actuation test before it counts as a hygromorph benchmark.

Get the paywalled HygroSkin/HygroScope papers (Reichert 2015; Menges & Reichert 2015) via the practice or a library before claiming to beat the Stuttgart apertures; the public page gives no thickness or cycle data.
